title: Hasan the peacemaker
hookLine: the elder grandson, who would one day make peace to spare blood

lines: A BOY BESIDE HIM ON THE PULPIT.
ONE LOOK TO THE CROWD, ONE TO THE BOY.
cards: The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is on the pulpit in Medina, speaking to the people. Beside him is a boy: al-Hasan, the son of Fatimah and Ali, his grandson.

As he speaks, he keeps turning, one look to the crowd, one look to the boy. Then he says something about the child that nobody in the room can check. It's a prediction, and it won't come true for years.
A companion named Abu Bakrah remembered it, and passed it on. Today: Hasan the peacemaker.

teach.h: THIS SON OF MINE IS A SAYYID.
teach.b: Here's what he said, in a report in Sahih al-Bukhari: this son of mine is a sayyid, a leader, and perhaps God will make peace through him between two great groups of Muslims. Perhaps. He doesn't say how, or when.
The same report, told by the scholar al-Hasan al-Basri, jumps forward to the grown man.
After the death of his father Ali, Hasan led battalions against Mu'awiyah that the narrator describes as like mountains.
One of Mu'awiyah's own men warned that those battalions would not turn back before they had killed their opponents.
Then messengers went between them with terms, and Hasan accepted. He stepped back from rule, and the two armies did not meet in that battle.

Al-Hasan al-Basri then adds the old memory: I heard Abu Bakrah say he saw the Prophet on the pulpit with Hasan beside him. Sunni and Shi'a Muslims read this moment in different lights, and both honor him.

In Sunni teaching the hadith is read as fulfilled, and his choice is praised. In Twelver Shi'a teaching Hasan is the second Imam, and the treaty is understood as a hard choice made to protect the believers' blood.
Either way, the picture is the same: a man with an army, and a claim, who could have pushed on, and chose the settlement instead.

teach.h: SULH: A SETTLEMENT BETWEEN TWO SIDES.
teach.b: The Arabic word for that kind of peace is sulh: a settlement, a making of peace between two sides.
Winning would have had a cost counted in lives. He chose not to pay it.

how: Muslims honor al-Hasan ibn Ali as the Prophet's grandson; Twelver Shi'a Muslims count him as the second Imam, and his settlement is cited as an example of choosing peace to spare lives.

o: a victory won by the side with the larger army
a settlement, a making of peace between two sides
a surrender, giving up every claim to the other

games.q: you're Hasan, at the head of battalions like mountains. messengers arrive with terms. what do you do?
o: march on and fight for your claim.
accept the terms and step back from rule.
send the messengers away and wait.
games.why: he accepted, and the two armies did not meet in that battle, as the Prophet had hoped: perhaps God will make peace through him.

practice: Bring to mind a disagreement that's still open, notice the part of you that wants to win it, and ask what a sulh would look like: not surrender, but a settlement where each side gives something.
Find the one thing you could give up, and hold it loosely. If you pray, ask God to make peace through you; if not, just rest with the thought of the argument ending.

wordCard.voice: Sulh, a settlement, the peace Hasan chose over battle when he stepped back from rule rather than pay for victory in lives. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a settlement, a making of peace between two sides.

carryVoice: Your line: the peacemaker. A settlement can be worth more than a win. Until tomorrow.
